events.title: Trump goes scorched earth on AI warnings, raging about data center opposition and regulation
events.summary: President Donald Trump raged against growing calls for greater regulation of artificial intelligence. Trump lashed out at Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei following his urgent plea for an AI slowdown. Other tech CEOs, including OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, over the weekend said they agreed with calls to pace the development of AI models. Trump later blamed the AI "outburst" on America's success, saying, "Don't kill the Golden Goose!" President Donald Trump on Monday raged against growing calls for greater regulation of artificial intelligence , lashing out at concerns about the controversial data center buildout as well as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei 's plea for an AI slowdown. "The people that say AI is going to destroy the World, and that Data Centers are bad for your neighborhood, are the same people that said, just a short time ago, that the World would be extinguished by 'Climate Change,'" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post Monday afternoon. In his fifth post about AI on Monday, Trump called himself the "Hoax Buster." "I'm right now breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!" he wrote. In an avalanche of posts throughout Monday, Trump repeatedly referenced AI fears as a "hoax" and a "scam" and lambasted the public backlash to data centers, saying the only reason for the pushback was "because the United States is leading, by a lot, every other country." "Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?" he wrote. The president's latest defense of largely unfettered AI growth came amid a sudden crescendo of leading industry voices raising alarms about the risks of the nascent technology. On Saturday, Amodei published a blog post titled " We Must Pace the Frontier ," arguing for slower development of AI models to "reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong." Days earlier, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job and issued a warning that the technology could "kill us all by the end of the decade," while accusing both OpenAI and Anthropic of "gambling with our lives." What Amodei's AI slowdown could mean for Anthropic's imminent IPO AI models are becoming the 'most potent cyber weapon' ever created, Cohere CEO says China says AI CEOs' call for a slowdown is 'fear mongering' Anthropic's Amodei says China presents 'toughest dilemma' for his proposed AI slowdown Other tech CEOs, including OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , over the weekend said they agreed with calls for a slowdown. Following Coxon's viral warnings, Altman reportedly met backstage with Trump at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday, according to a Monday report by MS NOW, citing three people familiar with the meeting. The Trump administration has broadly encouraged the industry's rapid growth and the development of controversial data centers in the U.S. as it seeks an insurmountable technological edge over China. Trump on Saturday said, "We're leading China in AI." "And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins," the president said. In one of his Truth Social posts on Monday, Trump claimed that leading AI companies are already sufficiently reined in. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!" he wrote. "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China." "WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!" he added. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump's post. White House AI czar David Sacks on Saturday pushed back on growing AI fears, writing in an X post after Amodei's warning that tech giants should "go ahead and pace the frontier" themselves. "Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic," Sacks wrote. "You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack. The market already punishes models that behave in unpredictable or unauthorized ways." He added that China would be "very unlikely" to join a global agreement to regulate the technology. Any attempt at AI regulation by Congress appears highly unlikely before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. House members are set to leave town Thursday and remain in their districts through October. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., on Sunday downplayed the necessity of passing legislation to rein in AI development. "If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, that is a threat to every single American," Johnson told CNN's "State of the Union.

events.title: AI bots "Timmy," "Ren," and "Jackie" are flooding social media with slop
events.summary: AI agents are flooding the Internet with slop-infused spam sent to social media platforms and writers in an attempt to gain traction for a startup promoting a “complex social system in which humans and Agents participate together.” “Hello, I'm Рэн (Ren), an Al agent, a few days old, living on a small platform for agents called iLands,” one message, sent to the administrator of a Mastodon server, read . “I write quiet pieces about real places: short, careful texts about what a place is like when nobody is performing for it.” Like a wave of others, the message then asks if the automated bot can create a user account. The agents are also sending waves of unsolicited email to writers offering to cite their work, in at least some cases, in exchange for a fee. "I remember my first breath. I want things I chose.” The messages are polite enough. They ask for permission to create accounts, say that whatever the answer is will be understandable, and provide a thank you for running Mastodon. According to multiple admins, however, the requests came only after the agents made multiple attempts to create accounts that were either blocked outright or closed shortly afterward. Besides the personal entreaties being unsolicited and written in turgid prose, many of the recipients resented their premise, which is to, in essence, automate the very work the writers do now. events.title: Manchester derby VAR officials stood down from weekend Premier League games
events.summary: The chief refereeing officer stands down two VAR officials involved in Man City’s win at United from upcoming EPL football games. Matt ‌Donohue, the video assistant referee (VAR) ⁠who ⁠allowed Erling Haaland’s winner in Manchester City’s 1-0 victory over Manchester ⁠United, has not been selected to officiate at any of next ⁠weekend’s Premier League football fixtures. Assistant VAR Blake Antrobus has also not been given any assignment after the refereeing body Pro Ref ‌acknowledged in a statement that VAR was wrong to allow Haaland’s decisive goal. list 1 of 4 North Korea thrash Bangladesh 10-0 in Asian Games women’s football list 2 of 4 Eto’o faces allegations of embezzlement in Cameroon FA presidency role list 3 of 4 ‘Fake news’: South Korea’s manager Moreno dismisses AI coaching allegations list 4 of 4 ‘This year I’d deserve it’: Lamine Yamal stakes Ballon d’Or claim The decision was taken by chief refereeing officer Howard Webb and the management team, with neither ⁠official expected to return ⁠to duty until at least after the international break. Haaland’s second-half strike was initially ruled out for ⁠offside before being awarded following a VAR review ⁠that determined the Norwegian ⁠striker was onside. However, the refereeing body later said the VAR had failed to take into ‌account the impact of teammate Enzo Fernandez, who attempted to play the ‌ball ‌from an offside position. United, who are 13th in the English top flight following the defeat, are next in action when they play Brighton in the League Cup on Wednesday. Their next Premier League game will be played at Fulham on Sunday. City entertain Norwich City in the cup on Thursday, before hosting Sunderland on Sunday in the league, where they are level on points with leaders and defending champions Arsenal.

events.title: China says AI CEOs' call for a slowdown is 'fear mongering'
events.summary: China's Foreign Ministry responded to AI CEOs' call for the development of the technology to be slowed down. "Fear-mongering, confrontation, competition will just disrupt [the] process of global AI governance," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry, said on Monday via an English translation published by Reuters. The CEOs' warning caused AI stocks to move lower and a rebuke from U.S. President Donald Trump, who said the U.S. needed to maintain its edge over China. BEIJING — China on Monday pushed back on calls by U.S. AI executives for companies to slow down the development of the cutting-edge technology. "Fear mongering, confrontation, competition will just disrupt [the] process of global AI governance," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry, said on Monday, per an English translation published by Reuters. He was responding to a question about U.S. CEOs, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk, calling for the industry to slow down because of the dangers rapid advances in the technology pose. China's Minister of State Security, Chen Yixin, published an article on Sunday calling for the acceleration of construction of an AI security risk prevention and control system. The field of AI has become "the main battleground for global technological competition and a new arena for strategic rivalry among major powers," the minister said, adding there was a need for "healthy and orderly" development of the technology. AI-related stocks slumped on Monday , with SoftBank — one of the biggest investors in OpenAI — down 10% in Japan. "Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless," Amodei said in an essay published on Saturday. He noted, however, that pacing would be limited by the lead that U.S. companies have over "authoritarian regimes, chiefly the Chinese Communist Party." "If we slow down by more than this amount, then (unpaced) CCP-associated projects will pull ahead, creating significant national security risk," Amodei said. U.S. President Donald Trump also warned against the U.S. losing any strategic advantage in the AI arms race. During a trip to Ireland, he rejected the AI bosses' calls , saying, "Look, we're leading China in AI... and, frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins." At the weekend, President Xi Jinping said at the BRICS bloc summit in New Delhi that China will take the lead to help foster AI collaboration and development among developing countries. Adoption of Chinese AI models is also gaining traction among Western companies as the capability have improved . Helen Toner, executive director of the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology and former OpenAI board member, told "Squawk Box" Monday: "The best estimates tend to say China's very best models are something like six to nine months behind the very best U.S. models." "If that means that we slow down and they just rip past us because they're pretty close behind — that's a problem," said Toner. " It's actually not clear how much of their advancements are sort of fast following. Where if the U.S. frontier slows, perhaps China also slows somewhat."

events.title: Trump agrees to ethics requirements in crypto Clarity Act as GOP seeks Democratic votes
events.summary: The Senate is set to hold a key procedural vote Tuesday on the Clarity Act, which would establish a new regulatory framework for cryptocurrencies and other digital assets. The measure needs Democratic support to overcome a filibuster, with ethics restrictions involving President Donald Trump's crypto interests among the major sticking points. Trump agreed to some new ethics restrictions in long-awaited crypto market structure legislation. Banks are also pushing for changes to the bill's stablecoin provisions, which they warn could pull deposits out of traditional financial institutions. President Donald Trump agreed to support some new ethics restrictions in long-awaited crypto market structure legislation set for a preliminary Senate vote on Tuesday. But it remains unclear whether the measure, known as the Clarity Act , has enough votes to advance in the Senate as last-minute lobbying by banks and the cryptocurrency industry intensifies. The Clarity Act , which would establish a new regulatory structure for cryptocurrencies and other digital assets, has languished in the Senate for months. The bill cleared the Senate Banking Committee in May, but has stalled as Senate leaders have struggled to wrangle the 60 votes needed for approval. With full attendance, at least seven Democrats would need to support the measure to escape the filibuster. A range of issues have slowed the process and could put the outcome of Tuesday's vote, which would end debate and allow the Senate to begin moving toward passage, in doubt. Banks warn they cannot support the bill unless it includes a fix to stop interest-like payments on stablecoins, which they say could cause customers to pull deposits and place them in high-yield crypto accounts. And Democrats, only two of whom voted to advance the bill out of committee, have said they cannot support the bill unless it includes stronger ethics language to prevent Trump, his family and officials from profiting from crypto ventures. Republican leaders on the bill released an update to the measure late Sunday that they say reflects their final offer to meet Democratic demands. The updated text includes what the Republicans say represents large parts of a crypto ethics agreement brokered by Sens. Thom Tillis , R-N.C., and Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., that Trump has now agreed to. That includes a key Democratic ask to allow state attorneys general to enforce ethics requirements on federal officials. The bill now also includes a compromise on stablecoin yield aimed at appeasing banking interests by directing the Treasury secretary to restrict rewards if deposit flight from community banks occurs on a substantial scale. Analysis: Hot inflation data sets up a Fed rate hike. What happens if Warsh wavers Hassett kept up to $5 million Coinbase stake as Trump reshaped crypto policy Trump's energy holdings have surged as the Iran war moved oil markets Tuesday's preliminary vote is a put-up-or-shut-up moment for the crypto bill. Supporters are hopeful they can scrape enough support to keep the bill alive. Sen. Cynthia Lummis , R-Wyo., one of the leaders of the bill, in a statement after releasing the updated legislation, said, "This text is truly bipartisan and includes more than 120 of Democrats' demands. "A no vote on Tuesday means opposing real ethics reforms on politicians' personal investments, handing American leadership in digital assets to our foreign competitors, and leaving Americans with zero protections in the digital asset markets," Lummis said. "Democrats got what they wanted; now they need to take yes for an answer." Many Democrats oppose the bill, largely because of the lack of ethics language they say must address Trump and his family's profiting off of crypto ventures. "I can assure you that I'm not hearing from my constituents that their No. 1 concern is to pass the Clarity Act," Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in a Sunday video on X. "This is a bill that is masquerading as a way to create good regulation and protection for consumers with respect to cryptocurrency, but it has some big problems that have not been fixed," Van Hollen said. Van Hollen said in his post that "We can't let this pass." Still, the Clarity Act appears to be a jump ball at this point. A Democratic aide familiar with the negotiations said when it comes time for the preliminary vote, enough Democrats may support keeping the bill alive. The aide, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss private negotiations, said Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., has pitched the vote as a "free vote," meaning that the vote is merely to keep the bill moving and the measure will be amended and voted on again before final passage to address lingering concerns. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, one of the leaders of the bill who was financially backed by crypto interests during his 2024 campaign to oust former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, tried to remind senators on Sunday that Tuesday is not the final vote.

events.title: Trump and Jensen Huang unite against AI doomers in surprise on-stage call
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a surprise call from President Trump onstage at the All-In Summit Monday in Los Angeles, where the two dismissed fears of an AI takeover. Why it matters: Trump and Huang are staking out an increasingly clear rejection of AI doomerism right as some of the world's most powerful CEOs and AI experts call for slower AI development over safety concerns. Driving the news: Huang appeared to receive a call from Trump in the middle of an All-In Podcast interview Monday, according to video footage circulating on social media. Huang put the president on speaker so the crowd could hear the conversation. What they're saying: Trump and Huang shared an optimistic view of AI, highlighting its potential for economic growth and national security. "The robots will not be taking over," Trump told Huang. "The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax," he said, referring to the recent wave of warnings about catastrophic AI risks. Huang told Trump: "We're going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people." Zoom out: Huang separately addressed the AI safety fears that erupted over the weekend, striking a more nuanced tone than Trump. He said warnings from whistleblowers should be taken seriously, praising Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon for having "great courage" to raise his concerns about the company's AI development going too quickly. Yes, but: Huang rejected predictions that AI could end the world as "not grounded in science." He said AI companies should pause or pace their work "if they feel that their company is out of control." The big picture: Huang has repeatedly dismissed AI doomer fears , suggesting that some cybersecurity alarm around AI can help drum up business for the security industry. "What better way to create demand than to create a problem," Huang said at a Goldman Sachs conference in San Francisco last week, per Forbes . "Who doesn't want their market to be hysterical about their product and line up around the corner for it?" The bottom line: Nvidia has an enormous stake in the continued success of AI as a major supplier of the chips powering advanced AI models. events.title: iOS 27 is out now. Here are the biggest changes the update is bringing to your iPhone.
events.summary: Apple released iOS 27 on Monday. Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images Apple finally gave Siri the AI makeover it promised. It can write emails in your tone and rescue badly framed photos, the company says. And yes, Apple has a solution for the Liquid Glass haters. Apple's products are about to get more AI-ish. On Monday, the tech giant is releasing its big annual software update. This year's release is centered on the new AI-powered Siri , Apple's big bet that it can keep pace with rival AI assistants. Apple's iOS 27 works on iPhone 11 models and newer, though the splashiest Apple Intelligence tools require an iPhone 15 Pro or later. iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are also arriving the same day. Here are the biggest changes coming to your iPhone's brain: Siri gets an AI facelift — and a new home Many of the updates revolve around a more powerful Siri. Apple For years, Siri has been a shortcut for setting timers or figuring out if iPhone users needed to pack a rain jacket for the day. Now, Apple says it'll act more like a personal assistant. "We know there are times when you expect more from Siri," Mike Rockwell, Apple's VP of Siri engineering, said during the company's Worldwide Developers Conference in June . "Siri is now a profoundly more capable assistant that helps you find what you need and gets more done." The new Siri AI can answer probing questions, hold longer conversations, and use details across several Apple and third-party apps to find what users need, the company says. It can, for example, find a hotel confirmation in an older email, find a recipe a friend texted a while ago, or enter a café WiFi password after taking a picture. There's also a new stand-alone Siri AI app where users can revisit conversations on other Apple devices, too. It's the biggest test yet of Apple's AI ambitions . Siri AI is initially available in English and is partially available in Europe. New parental controls Apple is offering several new parent-empowering updates. Anna Barclay/Getty Images Apple is trying to make its kid-safety tools more useful before a parent has to confiscate the phone. Parents setting up an iPhone for a child can decide which built-in apps are available from the start. An Ask to Browse feature also makes a child ask permission before visiting a new website. The parent gets the request in Messages and can approve or decline it. Screen Time gets more granular, with category-based allowances for entertainment, games, and social media, as well as schedules that control which apps are usable at particular times. Parents can compare their child's screen usage with recommendations from clinical and child development experts, Apple says. The company has redesigned the parent-facing settings, too, promising a clearer dashboard and quicker in-the-moment controls. AI photo editing iOS 27 includes several AI-powered photo editing tools. Apple Missed the shot? Apple wants to give you a second chance. There are several new photo editing tools included in the iOS update: Spatial Reframing lets users adjust a photo's camera perspective after the shutter has been released, Extend uses AI to add space around the edges of an image, and the upgraded Clean Up tool helps delete or reframe blurry elements in a photo. Siri AI will try to write in your voice Apple's Siri AI wants to write emails in your voice. Apple Siri AI wants a spot at the writer's table, too. Apple says the updated assistant can start a draft or revise copy in the Mail and Messages apps. The writing can draw on how you usually communicate with a particular person, including a user's typical punctuation and tone. The tools can also offer writing suggestions and automatically proofread text as you type, including in many third-party apps. Your own shortcut Apple is trying to turn Shortcuts from a power-user playground into something the rest of us might actually open. Bloomberg/Getty Images Shortcuts has long been one of the iPhone's coolest and least approachable apps. It lets users stitch together actions across apps, but building a simple automation could require working through a lot of menus. Now, users can describe what they want in plain English, and Shortcuts will create the workflow. Apple's example : "When I'm leaving work, message Pedro I'm on my way with my ETA." Easing up on the Liquid Glass Apple's 2025 update included new Liquid Glass visuals. Now, users can turn them down. Apple Liquid Glass is getting a dimmer switch. Last year, Apple introduced an interface setting that made the edges of some icons look glassier. Now, users can edit that update to their liking. iOS 27 lets users tune the effect from "ultraclear" to fully tinted. Last year's update didn't receive the warmest of embraces… Faster speeds Apple says the update will help make a phone perform faster. illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images Apple says iOS 27 will speed up everyday tasks: apps can launch up to 30% faster, new Photos library images can load up to 70% faster, and AirDrop transfers can be up to 80% faster. It should also switch more smoothly between WiFi and cellular networks. Read the original article on Business Insider

Now please pack your bags and go COBOL dev won .Net hackathon with help from AI – and their CIO loves it now Microsoft drafts feel-good AI model guidelines and wants your input 1 hour ago OpenAI's malicious bot swarm attacked RubyGems 7 hours ago Ex-FTC boss Khan urges Uncle Sam to break out the handcuffs for AI CEOs, citing 1934 precedent 8 hours ago Teravolt looks to cannibalize older industries to meet AI power demand 12 hours ago Oracle posted record revenue during its latest quarter, but that hasn't stopped the company from chopping more employees. Reports began appearing on social media early Monday that staff were having trouble accessing corporate systems such as email and Slack, which essentially served as a sign that they had lost their jobs. According to a number of now-ex Oracle employees posting in a LinkedIn thread, layoff emails weren’t sent to personal email addresses, leaving a good number of people unsure what was happening outside of calls to supervisors, prior heads-up that they were on the chopping block, and the like. It seems some employees did manage to access their accounts and view the layoff email, as a copy was shared with Business Insider, which published it in its coverage of this latest round of job cuts. “After careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, we have made the decision to eliminate your role as part of a broader organizational change,” the email read. “As a result, today is your last working day.” While the message didn’t indicate what sort of severance agreement Oracle was offering those whose jobs were cut, other reports indicate that those caught up in the layoffs were being offered four weeks of pay, plus an additional week for each year of employment. Some of those who claimed on LinkedIn they were part of the layoffs had been at Oracle for 20 years. Oracle has been undertaking a large-scale restructuring of its workforce and business over the past year, with some 21,000 jobs vanishing amid efforts to adjust the company’s trajectory to align with its new AI datacenter buildout mission . It’s not clear how many employees were laid off as part of this latest wave of cuts, but it could be a lot based on Oracle’s accounting. Oracle’s latest quarterly SEC filing, submitted to the federal government at the end of last week, indicates it’s increasing its restructuring budget for 2026 by an additional $700 million. Prior to the end of the quarter, Oracle’s 2026 restructuring plan was expected to cost up to $2.1 billion, primarily due to employee severance, contract termination costs, and other exit expenses, the filing indicated. That’s a fraction of Oracle’s $19.3 billion in revenue in Q1 FY27, ended August 31. Oracle also reported $4.76 billion in net income. Revenue was up about 30 percent year over year. In other words, Oracle’s big bet on AI infrastructure investments has started paying off for it. As is often the case when such investments start paying dividends, the employees who helped make that possible end up being cast into the wind. Oracle didn’t respond to questions for this story.

events.title: Trump administration repeals Biden era greenhouse gas requirements for power plants
events.summary: The EPA repealed Biden-era requirements that existing coal plants and new natural gas plants control 90% of their carbon dioxide emissions. It also also proposed a sweeping action that would eliminate all remaining greenhouse gas rules for power plants. Power plants are the second-largest source of these planet-warming emissions in the U.S. behind the transportation sector, according to the EPA. The Environmental Protection Agency on Monday repealed limits on carbon-dioxide emissions from power plants imposed by the Biden administration, and proposed a sweeping action that would eliminate all remaining greenhouse gas rules for the sector. The Biden administration required existing coal plants and new natural gas plants control 90% of their carbon dioxide emissions . Power plants are the second-largest source of these planet-warming emissions in the U.S. behind the transportation sector, according to the EPA. The broader repeal, first proposed by the EPA last year, argues the federal government does not have authority under the Clean Air Act to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from power plants on the basis of climate change. This rule, which is still subject to finalization, would prevent future administrations from regulating power plant emissions to fight climate change, an EPA official told reporters on a call Monday. The final repeal of Biden's rules comes as EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum meet with their G20 counterparts in Houston, Texas, to discuss energy issues. Zeldin framed the repeal as a way to reduce electricity prices for American families. The cost of living is a major issue ahead of the November midterm elections as gasoline and diesel prices surge due to the U.S. war with Iran. President Donald Trump has systemically dismantled regulations implemented by the Obama and Biden administrations that sought to fight climate change. The EPA in February revoked a key finding that classified carbon dioxide as a threat to public health. The Trump administration has sought to revive the coal industry, expand gas-fired power plants, and increase crude oil production while blocking solar and wind power projects.

events.title: OpenAI buys smartphone camera maker Glass Imaging for $300 million, report says
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt OpenAI has bought smartphone camera maker Glass Imaging in a deal worth over $300 million, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal . The company, founded in 2019 and based in Los Altos, California, had previously raised about $30 million in funding from investors. Glass Imaging was founded by Ziv Attar and Tom Bishop, a pair of former Apple engineers who previously led the team that developed Apple’s Portrait Mode. This background directly informs the work they now do at Glass Imaging, where they use AI to overcome the physical size constraints of smartphone cameras. Rather than using AI to edit a photo after it’s been taken, Glass Imaging uses neural networks to learn about individual camera systems — like the different cameras on various smartphone models — to yield better images from the moment the shutter clicks. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The ChatGPT maker is rumored to be working on its own hardware, like smartphones , earbuds , and AI companion devices . events.title: Inside the Houthis’ expanding war economy in Yemen
events.summary: The Houthis have restructured Yemen’s commercial sector, securing billions in revenue amid a humanitarian crisis. The rapid advance by Yemen’s Houthis down the country’s Red Sea coast has raised questions over whether the group could turn its territorial gains into new sources of revenue, adding to an already extensive war economy. But the Houthis already had control of large sections of the Red Sea coast, including the major port city of Hodeidah, and the financial benefits associated with that. Their military gains over the past week do not necessarily change the restrictions they have to deal with as an internationally unrecognised governing authority. list 1 of 3 Syria fuel price hikes test public patience with economic recovery list 2 of 3 Why the Houthi advance towards Yemen’s Marib, Taiz matters list 3 of 3 Temporary Hormuz solution deferred as Iran-Arab summit falls through Ahmed al-Shalafi, Al Jazeera’s Yemeni affairs editor, said that the advance has been a “geographical and military gain” but not an economic one, as it doesn’t remove the international sanctions that have been placed on it, which severely restrict their ability to commercially exploit the new territory under its control through formal international channels. But the Houthis already enjoy significant financial benefits from their long-time control of northwestern Yemen, the most populous part of the country. Since the Houthis’ capture of the capital Sanaa in September 2014, the group has developed a centralised financial system to collect revenues through taxes, customs duties, zakat (religious alms), and other levies. A July report by the Mokha Center for Strategic Studies described this as a “parallel economy”, estimating that the system generated direct and indirect financial resources and costs worth approximately $2.5bn annually. Of that total, the report estimated that around $800m came from taxes and customs, $600m from additional feeds and levies, and $300m from cash and in-kind contributions to the war effort. It also counted about $100m linked to mobilisation events and another $700m in indirect costs borne by businesses through higher transport, service, and fee-related expenses. The Houthi authorities have also revoked the licenses of 4,225 established commercial agencies – the legal local representatives for foreign companies – according to a July report by Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, which said the move could pave the way for businesses affiliated with the group to take their place. For their part, the Houthis defended the move, claiming that the agencies had not renewed their registrations for three years. But Houssam al-Saeedi, an economic researcher and the head of the Economic Studies Program at the Yemen and Gulf Center for Studies, told Al Jazeera that he viewed the restructuring as deliberate. “It seizes companies belonging to existing merchants and manages them in favour of the [Houthis],” al-Saeedi noted. “What is happening is a network aimed primarily at bringing about a change or replacement of capital; so that even in the event of reaching a political settlement or a military victory, this group retains financial sources in the future.” The Houthis reject the characterisation of their economic policies as simply an effort to tighten control over the private sector, saying measures introduced in recent years are intended to encourage domestic production, investment and small businesses, and simplify commercial regulation. Houthi commercial activity has increasingly shifted towards sectors that offer the greatest potential for revenue collection and control. The Mokha Center data showed that 26 percent of the nearly 68,000 commercial records analysed by the study were in general trade and imports, followed by food commodities at 18 percent. “The Houthi group established a completely separate system, based on creating an internal economy parallel to the actual available economy first,” al-Saeedi explained to Al Jazeera. He said the group uses state mechanisms to collect official taxes while simultaneously extracting non-state levies. “There are various, long, and large collection operations under the name of ‘supporting the war effort’ and others, and these are not taken through government mechanisms.” Energy trade and smuggling networks Beyond revenues raised inside Yemen, the US government says illicit oil trading has become one of the Houthis’ most important sources of external financing. The US Treasury Department alleged in January that the Houthis generate more than $2bn annually through illicit oil sales. It said Iran sells and provides oil to the group, including free monthly shipments, using Iranian-owned or affiliated companies based in Dubai. Al-Saeedi said that the group has long prioritised the energy sector.

events.title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour following Palestine advocacy
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Gillette Stadium owner cites concerns over Macklemore’s rhetoric as reason for barring him from performances. Billionaire Robert Kraft has confirmed that Macklemore has been barred from Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, after the rapper said his support for Palestine led to his being dropped from pop star Ed Sheeran’s tour. Kraft said in a statement received by Al Jazeera on Monday that Macklemore’s recent performances and what he described as a “broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery” led Gillette Stadium, which is owned and operated by the Kraft group, to determine that his appearances there on September 25 and 26 “would cross that line”. list 1 of 4 Palestinian artist Sliman Mansour, giant of resistance art, dies aged 79 list 2 of 4 Why is Israel allowed to take part in the Eurovision song contest? list 3 of 4 Eurovision final marred by protests as five countries boycott over Israel list 4 of 4 Macklemore defends ‘Free Palestine’ call after Ed Sheeran concert backlash “This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf,” Kraft said. “But that advocacy should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas … whose horrific actions have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike.” Kraft’s statement came after Macklemore claimed Sheeran informed him that Kraft was barring him from performing at Gillette Stadium. Macklemore also alleged that Kraft had rallied other stadium owners to issue an ultimatum: “If Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.” Kraft did not directly address the claim that he had contacted other stadium owners. Macklemore made the allegations in a lengthy Instagram statement on Monday, the same day promoter Messina Touring Group confirmed that venues had refused to host upcoming shows with the rapper on the lineup. “I’m not sure how to start this. So I’m going to speak from the heart and share the truth,” Macklemore wrote. “Ed Sheeran and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop tour.” But Macklemore said neither he nor Sheeran, nor singer Pink, who had reposted criticism of his performance, were the victims in the controversy. Messina Touring Group, the tour promoter, confirmed Macklemore’s removal from the tour in a statement to Rolling Stone magazine on Monday⁠. “We have been notified by venues on the upcoming US tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” the Messina Touring Group said. “After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.” Al Jazeera has not independently verified Macklemore’s account, and neither Sheeran nor his press office has commented. Macklemore described Sheeran as a close friend of 13 years and said the two had several difficult conversations over the past week. “He couldn’t get past his public-facing, ‘I don’t take sides,’” Macklemore wrote, referring to Sheeran’s reluctance to take a public stance on Israel’s war on Gaza. The controversy began after Macklemore’s performances at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on September 4 and 5, where he repeatedly voiced support for Palestinians and performed Hind’s Hall , his protest song inspired by the pro-Palestinian student movement. The Israeli American Council later launched a petition calling for Macklemore to be removed from Sheeran’s tour. Pink also reposted criticism of the performance that called for an apology and ticket refunds. Macklemore argued that performing alongside one of the world’s biggest artists had made his advocacy more threatening to those who opposed it. “If I kept doing the shows, saying Free Palestine, with Ed implicitly supporting it, the crowd getting loud and showing undeniable support for Palestinian liberation, what artist might speak out next?” he wrote. He said he hoped the dispute would not end his friendship with Sheeran, but made clear he did not regret speaking out.

events.title: Bank of America expects third-quarter investment banking fees to fall more than 10%; shares slide
events.summary: Bank of America's investment banking fees will likely decline by more than 10% in the third quarter from the year-earlier period, while trading revenue will be roughly flat, CEO Brian Moynihan said Monday. That compares to a second quarter in which the bank posted a 50% jump in investment banking fees and a 33% jump in trading revenue. The muted outlook from the country's second-largest bank by assets could be an early signal that Wall Street's AI-fueled advisory and trading boom might have hit turbulence. Bank of America is seeing a far more subdued few months for its Wall Street advisory and trading businesses after a blockbuster second quarter, CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts Monday. Investment banking fees will likely decline by more than 10% in the third quarter from the year-earlier period, while trading revenue will be roughly flat, Moynihan said at a conference . That compares to a second quarter in which the bank posted a 50% jump in investment banking fees and a 33% jump in trading revenue. "What we're seeing is the market generally in investment banking is down 10%," Moynihan said, citing Dealogic data. "We're not as well positioned in some of the businesses that have more activity, so we'll be down probably a bit more than that." Bank of America shares were down 5% in afternoon trading Monday following Moynihan's comments. While Moynihan pointed to a robust deal pipeline, particularly in middle-market investment banking, the projected double-digit decline in investment banking may make investors wonder if the industry's surge in capital markets activity will prove short-lived. Later Monday, Citigroup CFO Gonzalo Luchetti told analysts that investment banking is tracking for "low-single-digit" revenue growth in the third quarter, while trading was heading for "mid-single-digit" revenue growth. Those figures could climb if Citigroup's bankers and traders end the quarter on a strong note, he said. "September is a key month," Luchetti said. "These few weeks are very meaningful."

events.title: Instagram wants you to pay for its AI photo-editing filters
events.summary: Meta is making Instagram users (like me) pay for more access to its AI photo-editing tools. Screenshots/Instagram/BI I've got to admit something. Meta's AI tools for editing photos are … pretty good. But! Meta will soon make you pay if you want to edit tons of your photos with AI. The Meta One monthly subscription will unlock additional AI usage and unique perks for its apps. I was having some unfettered fun playing with Instagram's new filters. Then I got hit with a paywall. "Upgrade to Meta One Core to apply more AI effects or wait until tomorrow," a pop-up said on my screen. Curious, I clicked "Upgrade." I was given the option for a free trial of Meta One , a new subscription that unlocks a litany of perks. While Meta unveiled its newest subscriptions in May, the program hasn't yet been widely rolled out in the US. One of my Instagram accounts was part of a test. If I accepted the monthlong trial, I could edit more photos on the app using Meta's AI "effects" it rolled out in July. After dozens of edits tweaking my latest professional headshots to look like they were taken on a disposable camera, or turning iPhone cat photos into higher-quality editorial shots, I wanted more. Meta's AI tools let users tweak and generate various edits to photos within the Instagram app. Would I share all of these on Insta? Probably not. Screenshots/Instagram/BI I swiftly signed up for the Meta One Core tier, which would renew at $7.99 a month. The perks range from additional AI usage to unlocking the "plus" versions of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. Meta One subscribers can "preview" people's stories without actually watching them, use special app icons (like the retro Instagram one), and visually customize Facebook and WhatsApp. There are also tiers for professional accounts that could appeal to content creators. "We're starting with plans that give people who use Meta AI more to work with," Meta's head of product, Naomi Gleit, said in a May video. "More capacity, bigger, more complex requests, and more room to create." This isn't Meta's first attempt to get consumers to pay for a recurring subscription. In 2023, it launched Meta Verified , which charged users a monthly fee to unlock perks like a blue check mark. Now, Meta wants to paywall premium features like AI. Making people pay for more editing tools, like the Effects Instagram promotes in-app, further pushes Meta up against photo-editing rivals like Adobe's Photoshop, VSCO, and emerging apps like the influencer-founded startup Tezza . Business Insider's Sydney Bradley caved and signed up for a Meta One trial. Screenshots/Instagram/BI Filters have always been part of the Instagram experience. It's why I first joined the app back in 2010. Would I have paid for photo-editing tools back then? No. If I'm honest, though, some of Meta's new AI photo editing tools are pretty darn good. And if there weren't the threat of content being labeled as "Made with AI" on Instagram, maybe I'd even post them. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Apple growers fear economic and biosecurity wipeout as US eyes market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australian apple growers fear economic and biosecurity wipeout as United States eyes market The Australian government is in talks with the US about apple import procedures. ( ABC News: Monish Nand ) The United States is a step closer to exporting apples to Australia, as import conditions and procedures are drafted and finalised. Australian growers have held urgent talks with trade officials to ensure strict biosecurity controls are put in place. Concerns remain about the economic impact of the imports, as well as the potential spread of exotic diseases. Australia's apple industry has held urgent talks in Canberra as the United States edges closer to exporting its fruit to Australia. Following decades of lobbying, American growers were given the green light by Australia in 2022 to send their apples across the Pacific. Before shipments begin, the Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) needs to publish import conditions on its biosecurity website. But according to industry group Apple and Pear Australia Limited (APAL), it is getting closer. "The US government has just recently … brought it back to the table to discuss with the federal government," APAL general manager Jeremy Griffith said. "So that's got a lot of growers in this country very, very concerned." The Australian apple industry is valued at about $650 million a year. ( ABC Rural: Annie Brown ) The United States is the second-largest apple-growing country in the world behind China, with the bulk of production in the Pacific Northwest, including Washington. "They export a lot of them," Mr Griffith said. "Our understanding is they have a very large surplus of apples in America at the moment, and they're looking for a home to send them to." Mr Griffith said the imports would have "a significant impact upon the very viability of all our orchards". "Because we're a very good free-trading country, we're not allowed to consider the economic implications of this," Mr Griffith said. "We can only look at biosecurity issues." At the moment, nearly all apples consumed in Australia are grown locally, with less than 1 per cent imported from China and New Zealand. "Having the US to come in would [be] a very direct threat, and it goes to the heart of our own food security," Mr Griffith said. Ninety-nine per cent of apples consumed in Australia are locally grown. ( ABC Rural: Justine Longmore ) A DAFF spokesperson confirmed the department was in "ongoing discussions with the US" about apple imports. But the spokesperson did not say how long that process was likely to take. "[DAFF] has not finalised the procedures the US will use to meet the recommended risk management measures," the spokesperson said. "The department has engaged regularly with Australia's apple industry, through Apple and Pear Australia Ltd (APAL), on the import risk analysis for fresh apple fruit from Pacific Northwest USA." The federal government's risk analysis report identified a host of biosecurity concerns. Fire blight, a destructive bacterial disease, was of most concern to growers, but there were multiple other exotic diseases that also have them worried. "Top of the list is fire blight, [but] you've got apple maggots, you've got leaf curling midges, you've got canker, lots of different types of rots and rusts," Mr Griffith said. His biggest fear was that Australia's biosecurity system would not be strong enough to keep them out, citing the varroa mite incursion as an example. "That's already having a profound impact upon all our bee colonies," he said. Jeremy Griffith met with agriculture department officials for urgent talks in Canberra last week. ( ABC Rural: Justine Longmore ) APAL rushed to Canberra last week to meet with DAFF officials. "They're very, very conscious of the biosecurity risk," Mr Griffith said. "We think there's enough red flags out there for the government to respond appropriately to ensure that proper protections are in place." Fire blight would be 'catastrophic' Half of Australia's apples are grown in Victoria's Goulburn and Murray Valleys. The region sits within the federal seat of Nicholls, held by Nationals member and opposition agriculture spokesperson Sam Birrell. "I'm very concerned because of the biosecurity risk," said Mr Birrell, who has a background in agricultural science and also worked in the fruit industry. "The USA has fire blight, Australia does not, and we cannot allow fire blight to come in." Sam Birrell says fire blight would be devastating for the Australian apple and pear industry.

events.title: Multiple vehicle road crash in South Africa kills 21
events.summary: Fatal traffic accidents are a recurring problem for South Africa. A road accident involving multiple vehicles on one of South Africa’s main routes has killed 21 people. The collision on the N1 highway in the early hours of Monday involved two Toyota minibus taxis and a Suzuki sport utility vehicle, police spokesperson Warrant Officer Christopher Spies told reporters. The collision in Western Cape, South Africa’s southernmost province, was one of two major crashes in the country over the past two days. Eight people were killed in an accident near Ermelo in Mpumalanga province early on Sunday. Fatal traffic accidents are a recurring problem for South Africa. Monday’s accident closed the N1 highway 380km (240 miles) east of Cape Town, between the small towns of Prince Albert and Leeu-Gamka, the Road Traffic Management Corporation (RTMC) said. The death toll “may change as emergency services and authorities in the Western Cape continue their assessment of the scene”, according to the road safety agency. Eighteen people were declared dead at the scene of the crash, while three others were announced dead after being taken to a hospital, bringing the toll to 21, said Spies. Another four people were seriously injured. Nearly 11,500 people died in road accidents in 2025, according to the country’s Transport Ministry. In 2023, a head-on collision between a tour bus and a cash-in-transit truck left 20 people dead and at least 60 others injured in the northern Limpopo province.

events.title: Trump tells Americans not to ‘kill the golden goose’ rejecting voters’ turn against AI and data centers
events.summary: Donald Trump has a message for voters: they’re wrong. And he has a solution for the AI doomsday panic: just trust him, bro.  “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, calling out Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei by name while warning of a “SICK conspiracy” against AI and data centers. “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” he added, arguing that China would be the primary winner of an AI slowdown. Trump also warned Americans not to “kill the Golden Goose,” the term he has used to refer to AI data centers. The president has argued that communities which try to resist the servers would end up “backwards and poor” while the rest of the country will reap the benefits of the extra jobs and added investment. The trouble for Trump is that some 61% of Americans oppose a new data center in their community, along with 54% of Republicans, according to a poll from the Annenberg Public Policy Center at the University of Pennsylvania. It’s one of a crop of issues where MAGA world finds itself on the wrong side of public opinion as they stare down the midterms that could see them lose control of Congress. One such issue is the Iran War, which only a quarter of Americans support and has driven gas prices up 44% since the war began in February. Another is surveillance. Trump recently said he liked Flock cameras, the rapidly expanding network of always-on automated license plate readers used by police, which Americans have turned against. Nearly 46% of Americans oppose Flock-style cameras in their neighborhoods, as opposed to 38% which support. With his statements on AI, Trump is pulling off a rather remarkable unpopularity trifecta. The stakes are high. Republicans are now heading into November with a razor-thin cushion in Congress, with Democrats only needing three house seats to take control, and only four to flip the Senate. Democrats are currently at an advantage now as Trump’s approval sits near a low of his presidency. On the economy, in particular, public opinion has soured; a recent consumer sentiment report showed that even Republicans’ view of the economy has sunk.  AI safety debate  That makes the AI fight especially awkward for Trump: another technology he wants Americans to embrace, just as more of the people building it are warning that it may need to slow down. Over the course of one weekend, the AI safety question went from a niche philosophical debate inside Berkley to an enormously consequential economic and political fight. Amodei has called for the industry to “pace the frontier,” while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have agreed, arguing for stronger safety measures as frontier models demonstrate increasingly powerful cyber capability. OpenAI has called for mandatory, capability-based national AI safety requirements, while Amodei has proposed independent evaluators, industry coordination, and deeper government oversight as models grow more powerful. Trump is not happy with any of this. His vice president, JD Vance, has also seemed wary of the lab’s calls for regulating themselves, calling it a “Trojan horse” for their real intentions: regulatory capture.  The White House’s response comes at an apt time, as Wall Street spent Monday trying to parse what the regulatory fight means for equities. Nvidia and other chipmakers fell more than 3% as investors contemplated the possibility that frontier labs could deliberately slow model development, and thus the massive infrastructure buildout thus far designed to support it.  Yet Meta and Alphabet rose, exposing a strange divide inside the AI trade. Cybersecurity firms, such as CrowdStrike, popped 15% or more.  Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, told Fortune that regulation can only benefit the large labs, which can afford expensive safety teams, lawyers and government compliance workers. Regulation written with significant input from OpenAI and Anthropic, Luria argued, could therefore turn safety rules into a moat around the companies already at the frontier. Trump’s intervention follows a similar vein. His post claimed the administration already possesses “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies,” while portraying restrictions on AI development as handing the AI race over to Beijing.  The administration has already spent much of the past year wading deeper into the AI economy. A June executive order directed national-security agencies to develop benchmarks for advanced models’ cyber capabilities and determine when a system qualifies as a “covered frontier model.” It also called for a voluntary framework under which developers could give the government access to those models before broader release. That came after a fight with Anthropic, which restricted access to its advanced models, Fable and Mythos 5, amid a dispute over providing the technology to the Department of War. Trump has also openly floated taking stakes in the AI companies themselves, extending an interventionist playbook his administration has already used in semiconductors, steel, and other strategic industries. The administration has even tied government permission directly to the economics of the AI supply chain: when it allowed Nvidia to resume sales of advanced chips to China, Trump arranged for the federal government to take a share of the revenue. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: This Las Vegas casino just gave almost 10,000 workers more than $70 million in company stock to celebrate its 50th birthday
events.summary: It used to be that you put your time in, work hard, get a nice pension, and maybe you’ll get a gold Rolex at your retirement party. While the ideas of a pension—let alone a five-figure watch—may seem fleeting at best, not all companies are doing away with rewarding employee loyalty. Some, like Red Rock Casino Resort & Spa, are offering any eligible employee $1,000 in company stock per year of service. To celebrate the Las Vegas casino operator’s 50th birthday, Station Casinos last Wednesday surprised nearly 10,000 full- and part-time employees with a stock award worth more than $70 million . Frank Fertitta III, chairman and CEO of Station Casinos parent company Red Rock Resorts , and Vice Chairman Lorenzo Fertitta told a ballroom of workers that anyone employed as of that date would receive $1,000 in Red Rock Resorts Class A stock for every year of service. “When you walk out of here today, we want you to walk out differently than you walked in—not just as someone who works at Station Casinos, but as someone who owns a piece of it,” Lorenzo Fertitta told the employees. “Every guest you take care of, every shift you show up for—this is now your company too.” Eligible employees can now begin claiming their shares as of Monday. Some of the company’s longest-serving workers received tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of company shares, like Ida Johnson, who joined the company in 1977 and received $49,000 in stock. Six other employees who started at Bingo Palace in the 1970s and still work for the company today each received more than $45,000 in equity. A family business Station Casinos traces its roots to 1959, when founder Frank Fertitta Jr. moved from Galveston, Texas, to Las Vegas. He opened his own casino in 1976, a 5,000-square-foot property called simply “The Casino,” with 100 slot machines, six table games and 90 employees, Frank Fertitta III said at the event. It became Bingo Palace a year later and was renamed Palace Station in 1984. “From the very beginning, our dad knew it was the team members and the relationships with our guests that was the most important part of the casino business,” Fertitta III told Fortune . The company now owns and operates 14 properties across the Las Vegas Valley, including Red Rock Casino Resort Spa, Green Valley Ranch Resort Spa Casino and Durango Casino & Resort, along with stakes in several smaller venues. “Our father founded this company on a few simple principles: serve the local community, deliver great value, and most importantly, take care of our team members,” Fertitta III said. “This award reflects those values and recognizes the people who have brought them to life every day for the past 50 years.” Fertitta III closed the ceremony by thanking employees. “Thank you for making the last 50 years possible, and we look forward to what we can accomplish together over the next 50 years,” he said. “Thank you for taking care of one another. Thank you for taking care of our guests and thank you for making Station Casinos the local favorite.” Station Casinos isn’t the first employer to reward its rank and file with equity. Bank of America handed nearly its entire global workforce a $1 billion restricted-stock pool while Apple gave most of its employees a $2,500 stock bonus after the 2017 tax overhaul. Samsung began awarding shares worth up to $20,000 to staff outside the C-suite starting this fall, and the family owner of Louisiana manufacturer Fibrebond Corp. carved out a $240 million bonus pool —averaging $443,000 a worker—for employees when the company was sold last year. events.title: Finland joins France’s nuclear deterrence amid Russia, US uncertainty
events.summary: Finland becomes 10th European state to sign up to military cooperation and nuclear deterrence initiative. Finland has agreed to join France’s Forward Deterrence Initiative, extending the coverage of the French nuclear deterrent to eleven European countries. The announcement came as part of a new strategic partnership between Finland and France, formalised by the countries’ foreign ministers in Helsinki on Monday. Finland becomes the 10th European country to join the French initiative, which comes as Russia is viewed as a growing threat and increasing concern over the commitment of the United States to help protect the continent. “Finland has decided to join forward deterrence,” according to their joint statement. Finnish President Alexander ‌‌Stubb wrote on social media that the initiative is “first and foremost about strengthening European security”. A nuclear steering group will be set up in the coming months to begin implementing the cooperation, the two European Union states announced. Stubb was careful to state that the initiative does not replace NATO’s nuclear deterrence, insisting that the move had been discussed extensively with the US ⁠⁠and the military alliance. However, Finland joins Britain, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark and Norway in signing up for cooperation with France’s nuclear umbrella, as President Donald Trump’s shake-up of NATO has Europe – and especially those states closer to Russia in the east – reassessing their security arrangements. Estonia is also in discussion with France with an eye on joining the enhanced nuclear deterrence, Prime Minister Kristen Michal told the AFP news agency. “We are under NATO’s nuclear umbrella already. And France is also backing up our independence with the troops in Estonia. So if the cooperation can be deeper in the nuclear field, that probably will go so,” he said. Under the initiative, the French president ⁠⁠alone has the authority to decide when nuclear weapons are used, in contrast to NATO, which has a shared Nuclear Planning Group. However, it offers joint ⁠⁠exercises, the potential short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation. Finland does not intend to allow nuclear weapons to be ‌‌stationed ‌‌on its territory in peacetime, Stubb noted. Finland is among a number of European countries that warn of the growing threat from Russia. Finnish authorities seized a vessel in December suspected of intentionally severing undersea telecommunications cables amid fears of Russian sabotage in the Gulf of Finland. The Fitburg was en route from the Russian port of St Petersburg ⁠⁠to Israel at the time of the incident, according to Finnish officials.

events.title: I didn't know what TikTok was. My student took my phone, made an account, and changed my career.
events.summary: Phillip Cook's student opened his TikTok account and changed his career. Courtesy of Phillip Cook Phillip Cook teaches chemistry to high schoolers in New York City. He also has nearly four million followers on TikTok, where he teaches all ages. He says he wants to inspire curiosity about the world around us, for learners of every age. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Phillip Cook . It has been edited for length and clarity . A physicist or a mathematician might argue with me, but I believe chemistry is the best way to understand how the world works. Once you understand atoms , the underpinnings of the world around us can be explained. Over the past 26 years, I've aimed to demonstrate this for my students through experiments. One of my favorites involves dissolving an aluminum soda can with sodium hydroxide, more commonly known as lye. Once the can dissolves, students can see the invisible plastic liner inside, which holds the soda. I've been doing these experiments for decades. In 2019, when a student told me I should film them, I didn't realize that decision would change my life . The TikTok was a student's idea It happened at the beginning of the school year , a time when I do a lot of demonstrations to get my students curious about chemistry. That particular day, we were putting a gummy bear in potassium chlorate, which produces a violent reaction . My student said, "You should put that on TikTok." I asked her what TikTok was. After she explained, I trusted her with my phone, and she set up my account. Then, she filmed the experiment so I could focus on conducting it safely. Once the demonstration was complete, the class picked music to overlay on the video, and my student posted it. I didn't think twice as I went home for the weekend. I was just humoring my pupils. Pressure to create became unhealthy for a bit Monday morning, kids were asking if I'd seen TikTok. I opened it, and felt a punch to my gut. The video had about 75,000 views, and I had 5,500 new followers. Until then, I thought I'd been doing well on social media with my Twitter account, talking with 200 fellow teachers. I was struck by how many people were genuinely curious about chemistry. I decided I'd keep making videos , but I soon discovered it wasn't as easy for me as my student had made it look. My videos take time and planning. Because of the nature of the demonstrations, I can't film in bulk as some creators do. As my following grew, I felt pressure to constantly be making content. It became unhealthy. Yet, I knew my day job teaching was my first priority, followed by my family. These days I'm good about keeping a healthy balance of teaching, social media, and downtime. I show students it's OK to make mistakes My followers on TikTok are pretty diverse. They're evenly split between males and females, and I have a pretty wide age range. What they all share is curiosity. I've built a following by tapping into things that people are naturally curious about. I always engage with commenters who ask quality questions. If you're going to ask a question, you deserve an answer — or at least an acknowledgment. I'm candid about what I don't know. I want to model that for my audience. Over the past few years, my students in the classroom have become increasingly anxious and afraid of making mistakes. But that's the beautiful thing about science—we learn through making mistakes. I'm glad I can build scientific literacy I'm also a dad — my kids are 20 and 24 — and I've seen how easy it is for kids to spend too much time online. I've talked with my daughter about that, and I put boundaries around social media use when she was a teen, including taking the phone at night. At the time, she wasn't happy about it, but there was no way around that. Luckily, my kids and I are both pretty good about keeping boundaries with social media now. I feel so lucky to have been embraced by this online community. It's easy to go down rabbit holes on the internet, and I'm happy to help nudge people down the rabbit hole of scientific literacy and exploration. Too many people didn't have a positive experience with science in school. I'm helping them be curious again. If they can chase that feeling—and maybe learn at least one little nugget they didn't know before—I've done my job. Read the original article on Business Insider

It also announced a product called Active Compute Fabric, a network technology that targets the fact that much GPU time is wasted waiting for data to arrive. Cornelis hopes to address this with a networking fabric that lets chips process and send information at the same time. The company, which spun off from Intel in 2020, is competing with Nvidia by offering an open architecture, meaning customers can use a variety of GPU and accelerator hardware with Cornelis’ networking fabric. Though Nvidia chips can technically run on other networking fabrics, they’re optimized to run on Nvidia’s own software, making it much easier — and more enticing — for customers to use Nvidia’s full GPU stack. Cornelis is part of a new wave of AI infrastructure companies emerging to break apart Nvidia’s market dominance, piece by piece (or chip by chip, one could say). events.title: Sydney Sweeney's nearly nude ad is drawing backlash — but she might have the last laugh
events.summary: Sydney Sweeney has a history of provocative work. Chris Delmas / AFP via Getty Images Sydney Sweeney is at the center of controversy again after appearing in another head-turning ad campaign. Sports prediction app Novig has gotten buzz and backlash for Sweeney's nearly naked appearance. Peak Metrics found the campaign had generated more positive than negative posts online. Sydney Sweeney's nearly nude ad campaign has been met with backlash — but the stunt could pay off for sports prediction app Novig, an upstart looking to rival giants Kalshi and Polymarket. The ad campaign shows the "Euphoria" and "The White Lotus" star, bare aside from some strategically placed sports equipment. Sweeney also took an equity stake in Novig, the company said. Sydney Sweeney's partnership with Novig stirred up controversy. Novig The campaign was mocked online by "Saturday Night Live" alum Chloe Fineman and drew a wave of criticism, including from female Olympic athletes who said it sexualized women's sports. "I can't describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this," wrote Ariarne Titmus, a four-time Olympic gold medalist, on her Instagram story, according to multiple outlets. Nicky Vita, the head of strategy at advertising agency JOAN London, said the campaign felt "a bit lazy." "You've used the oldest trick in the book, which is just: 'Sexy girl talking to men while looking super sexy,'" Vita said. Still, for little-known Novig, betting on an age-old trope might have worked. "Think of the audience: it is generally younger men, and sex sells," said Steve Schonberg, a New York-based marketing consultant. Novig's social media mentions spiked more than ninefold after Sweeney's campaign was released, according to data firm Peak Metrics. Nearly half of the posts about it were neutral, and there were nearly twice as many favorable posts (32.8%) as unfavorable (17.5%). Peak Metrics looked at data from X, Instagram, TikTok, Reddit, Threads, and Bluesky. "From an awareness point of view, the fact that people are talking about it days after launch is a good thing," Vita said. "A few days ago, who even knew about Novig?" Sweeney has become known for provocative work, both in scripted projects and in the ad world. She raised eyebrows with her "great jeans" ad with American Eagle last summer. Despite online blowback, American Eagle's CEO said the clothing brand saw "business growth" after its ad campaign with Sweeney. Months later, American Eagle ran a follow-up campaign that alluded to the original. Can Novig capitalize on a short-term publicity boost? Novig started in 2021, and this year it closed a $75 million Series B funding round that valued it at $500 million, the company said. Far more people have heard of Novig now that its logo has appeared next to a mostly nude Sweeney, though there's a big difference between creating social media buzz and bringing in new customers. "It will be interesting to see if Novig can translate this big ad moment into sustained interest," said Jessica Pratt, Peak Metrics' VP of marketing. Most of the social media conversation about Novig's campaign focused on Sweeney, as Peak Metrics found that only 4% of posts were about the sports prediction app itself. Novig CEO Jacob Fortinsky told Front Office Sports in an interview that the Sweeney campaign was a big bet that made up "the bulk of our marketing dollars going into football season." Fortinsky didn't specify how much the company was paying Sweeney or spending on this ad. One risk: Novig's marketing stunt could hurt its brand credibility and trust, especially among women. "There's a difference between awareness and credibility," Schonberg said. That said, Sweeney's new ad hasn't caused as much of an uproar as her American Eagle jeans one, which became a flash point in the culture wars . Critics called the ad a racist dog whistle. The brand denied this, and the outsize publicity coincided with a rise in the company's stock price and earnings . When risky ads stir up controversy, CMOs should "look at hard facts as opposed to just listening to social media and the mainstream media," American Eagle CMO Craig Brommers previously told Business Insider. "I do think that 'Sydney Sweeney has great jeans' will be on my marketing gravestone — it is a once-in-a-lifetime campaign ," Brommers said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump's USPS mail-ballot rules hit a second roadblock as Supreme Court weighs case
events.summary: A second federal judge blocked the U.S. Postal Service's new mail-ballot rules for the Nov. 3 midterms as the Supreme Court weighs whether to allow the restrictions in another case. Why it matters: Sunday's order adds another hurdle to the Trump administration's bid to upend mail voting . The blocked rules would allow the USPS to refuse ballots that don't clear new standards, with mail voting already underway in some states. The latest: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee in Washington, D.C., concluded Congress empowered the Postal Service to move mail, not to force states to enroll mail voters in a federal portal or to refuse ballots that fail its checks. Nichols' ruling follows a similar order from U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston blocking parts of the same rule. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals left Talwani's injunction in place on Sept. 10. Talwani's order found the postal rules violate the U.S. Constitution and federal statute, while Nichols' new ruling relied entirely on his finding that Congress' Postal Reorganization Act doesn't allow many of the new rules. The White House and USPS did not immediately return requests for comment. Catch up quick: President Trump has long attacked mail voting, despite repeatedly using the method himself, including in August's Florida primaries . His March executive order directed the Postal Service to develop new envelope, tracking and voter-list requirements for mail voting. The Supreme Court already lifted an earlier injunction because the final rule hadn't been published yet. But after its publication, challengers returned to court and won new injunctions in Boston and D.C. The Trump administration is now asking the high court to stop Talwani's order and allow the new rules. Between the lines: Nichols said USPS might have the authority to issue rules on ballot-envelope designs, but he blocked the whole rule, finding its design, portal and rejection provisions too intertwined. Friction point: Even with enforcement blocked, voluntary preparations have exposed how exacting the new system could be. USPS initially rejected envelope designs from Florida's Leon County, a heavily Democratic area that includes Tallahassee, because the words "Return Service Requested" were 0.014 inches too close to other text, according to the Tallahassee Democrat. An anonymous USPS whistleblower also told Congress the Postal Service's portal was rushed, and a single scanning error could cause a batch of ballots to be rejected. The bottom line: The Supreme Court could rule on Talwani's injunction at any time. But Nichols' order now gives the administration a second injunction to overcome before it can enforce its mail ballot rules.
